history: Futebol came to Portugal with the game itself, in the late nineteenth century, through British residents, sailors and students. At first the English spelling was used, foot-ball. Then the word was written as it is said in Portuguese, and became futebol: foot became fute-, and ball became -bol. Portuguese football is full of such English words, partly adapted. In Portugal the goalkeeper is the guarda-redes, ‘net-guard’, and a goal is um golo. In Brazil they say goleiro and gol, so here the two varieties really part ways. A match is um jogo, and the three big clubs, Benfica, Sporting and Porto, are simply os três grandes, ‘the big three’.
historyEinfach: Futebol means ‘football’. The word comes from English: foot + ball. The British brought the game to Portugal in the 1800s. In Portugal a goal is um golo; in Brazil it is um gol. The goalkeeper in Portugal is the guarda-redes.

elsewhere.text: Portuguese spells the English word the way it sounds in Portuguese.
Italy kept its own word for the game, ‘kick’, instead of borrowing football.
